newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia PM backs minister, but dismisses coup talk.
newsitem.headline: Russia PM backs minister, but dismisses coup talk.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, seeking to defuse a bitter Kremlin power struggle, gave partial backing to foes of Alexander Lebed on Thursday but dismissed allegations that Russia's security chief was plotting a mutiny or a coup d'etat.
Speaking after an emergency meeting of top security officials, Chernomyrdin said there was much truth in some of the accusations against security chief Lebed, a paratroop general.

But he rejected Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov's main charge -- that Lebed planned a "creeping coup" against the Moscow authorities and he said he was "far from thinking about mutinies and putsches".

Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin on Thursday as attacking "home-grown Bonapartism" -- a charge traditionally levelled at Russian generals such as World War Two hero Marshal Georgy Zhukov who are accused of excessive political ambition.
The flare-up in the Kremlin infighting comes two days after ailing President Boris Yeltsin told members of his team to stop squabbling and start working together.
Yeltsin, who faces an operation on his heart next month, may now have to choose between the two long-standing rivals.
His press office said on Wednesday that the president was worried about the accusations and had asked Chernomyrdin to explain what was going on.

Kulikov, an army general, made his allegations at a news conference on Wednesday and said Chechen gunmen would help Lebed seize power. "(Lebed) has decided to move ahead using force instead of waiting for the next presidential poll," he said.
Lebed, a reserve general in the elite Russian paratroop forces, denied the charges. RIA news agency said on Thursday he had asked Yeltsin for a personal meeting.

Lebed and Kulikov have been at odds since Yeltsin appointed Lebed his personal security adviser after the first round of the presidential election. Lebed asked Yeltsin to sack Kulikov in August, but the president declined.
The power struggle comes at a bad time for Yeltsin, who has spent only a few hours in the Kremlin in the 100-plus days since he won a second term in office.
It has already hurt nervous Russian financial markets, where share prices fell after Kulikov's accusations.
"There was panic in the morning," said one trader. "The market is very sensitive to political news."
But visiting U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said he remained confident in democracy in Russia.
"The Russian people have selected a democratic government... and I have great confidence that they will continue to weather any problems that come up," Perry said.
The president, currently in a sanatorium outside Moscow, met Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko on Wednesday, but he moved slowly in brief television footage.
Aides have denied all reports that he is out of touch, and doctors say the operation will go ahead as scheduled in the middle of next month.
Chernomyrdin is one of few people to meet Yeltsin regularly and he will take over briefly when Yeltsin has his operation.
The prime minister said on Thursday that security was being stepped up in "especially dangerous places" but gave no details.
A Moscow police source said an order for increased security measures had been received but not yet been activated.
Kulikov said on Wednesday that tougher security measures would help cope with what he said was a threat of attacks by rebels from the breakaway Chechnya region.
There have been many such alerts since Russia sent troops into the Caucasus region in December 1994 to crush its independence bid.

But Chechen gunmen have launched only two raids outside their borders, seizing hostages in a hospital in the southern Russian town of Budennovsk in June last year and carrying out a copy-cat raid in Kizlyar in autonomous Dagestan.
Dozens of people, mostly civilians, were killed in the raids.
Fighting in Chechnya has stopped after Lebed agreed a peace deal with the separatists. Kulikov and others have said the deal is tantamount to a capitulation by Moscow.
